Acute Limb Ischemia

Slide 2
  • Acute Limb Ischemia (ALI) is sudden decrease in limb perfusion causing a potential threat to limb viability.
  • Acute Arterial Occlusion , sudden decrease blood supply.
  • Most concerning symptom in acute limb ischaemia → paraesthesia (nerve ischaemia = threatened limb). 435
  • Presentation of acute critical limb ischaemia among the options → paralysis. 438
Notes

Acute Limb Ischemia

Sudden loss of arterial perfusion to a limb. Find the cause, read the 6 Ps, anticoagulate and revascularize, then anticipate the complications of reperfusion.

  • Acute limb ischaemia → IV heparin + revascularization. 437 ×2
  • After revascularization of a traumatic ischaemic leg — the reperfusion complication → hyperkalaemia. 436

Slide 4

  • Skin & Bone : Relatively resistant to ischemia

Notes

Clinical Assessment

CLASSIC VIGNETTE

60-year-old woman with AF on warfarin, who stopped warfarin a week ago for a dental procedure, presents with 2 hours of severe right-leg pain. Sudden severe unilateral pain + embolic risk factor → think embolic ALI. Examine and compare both limbs:

Color / pallor

Temperature (affected side colder)

Pulses at every level

Sensory & motor function

Pulse Examination Localizes the Occlusion

Pulse findingLikely level of occlusion
Femoral present, distal pulses absentDistal to the palpable femoral pulse, e.g. femoropopliteal segment
One femoral pulse absentIpsilateral iliac / proximal arterial occlusion
Both femoral pulses absentDistal aorta / aortic bifurcation

Vascular Emergencies · Study Guide

  • AF after an MI, sudden pale painful right leg, femoral pulse present, absent below, normal left leg → urgent embolectomy. 439 ×2

Notes

Clinical Presentation: The 6 Ps

Pain Sudden, severe, usually unilateral; develops over hours EARLY: PAIN · PALLOR · PULSELESSNESS · COLDPallor Pale compared with the opposite limbPulselessness Absent distal pulsesPoikilothermia Cold limbParesthesia Sensory loss from ischemic nerve injury SENSORY FIRSTParalysis Motor loss: very late, severe THEN MOTOR

DANGER SIGNS

Complete paralysis = advanced, potentially irreversible ischemia; amputation may be required.
Prolonged complete ischemia (e.g. ~15 h after severe trauma / tourniquet use) → extensive necrosis; reperfusion then releases accumulated toxic metabolites into the circulation and can be fatal.

Etiology

Slide 9
  • Arterial embolism
  • Acute arterial thrombosis
  • Arterial injury
  • Acute arterial dissection
Notes

Etiology: Three Causes

Embolus occludes the artery, commonly from a cardiac source, e.g. atrial fibrillation (AF), especially after anticoagulation is interrupted.
Lodges in a previously normal artery: no significant atherosclerosis, no collaterals → sudden, severe ischemia.
More common in veins (DVT) than arteries; same predisposing factors. Iatrogenic: femoral puncture / sheath for cardiac catheterization → local thrombus → leg pain within 1–2 h. Acute-on-chronic: PAD plaque ruptures → thrombosis → sudden complete occlusion.·Penetrating: laceration / transection or thrombosis → flow interrupted. Blunt: internal arterial injury, often with intact overlying skin. Knee dislocation → popliteal artery intimal tear / flap / dissection → thrombosis. Wall layers: intima, media, adventitia.
Embolism
Thrombosis·Trauma

Virchow's Triad (arterial and venous thrombosis)

Hypercoagulability

acquired or hereditary thrombophilia, e.g. antiphospholipid syndrome

Vascular Emergencies · Study Guide

PITFALL: ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC ISCHEMIA CAN LOOK DECEPTIVELY MILD

Chronic stenosis lets collaterals develop → some blood supply persists despite acute occlusion.
Symptoms are often less severe or atypical; the patient is used to chronic ischemic pain.
May not present with the full 6 Ps → diagnosis is harder.

Arterial Embolism

Slide 10
  • Embolic occlusion of a previously unobstructed vessel generally results in the most severe forms of acute ischemia
  • Suspected in patients with :
  • Acute onset , no intermittent claudication
  • +ve risk of embolism
  • Unilateral abnormal finding
Notes

Acute Embolism vs Acute-on-Chronic Thrombosis

FeatureAcute embolismAcute-on-chronic thrombosis
Previous arterial diseaseUsually absentPre-existing PAD / atherosclerosis
Previous ischemic symptomsUsually absentChronic history of pain / ischemia
Embolic sourceOften present, e.g. AFUsually absent
OnsetSudden, abruptAcute worsening of chronic disease
SeverityUsually severe, typical ischemiaMay be less dramatic (collaterals)
Collateral circulationUsually absent / poorOften well developed
Signs of chronic ischemiaAbsentOften present
Arterial pathologyAbrupt occlusion of a previously normal arteryThrombosis over an atherosclerotic stenosis

KEY RULE

Embolism causes worse ischemia because collaterals have not developed; acute-on-chronic occlusion may keep some supply through collaterals. Both are acute occlusions, but the underlying pathology changes investigation and revascularization planning.

Added explanationAcute mesenteric ischaemia: embolic (AF, recent MI — the commonest, lodges in the SMA just beyond the middle colic origin) · thrombotic (on atherosclerosis; history of postprandial pain) · non-occlusive (NOMI) — low-flow states: septic/cardiogenic shock, vasopressors, digoxin · mesenteric venous thrombosis. Pain out of proportion to examination, then peritonitis; ↑ WBC and lactate. CT angiography is the investigation of choice. Treatment: resuscitation, heparin, laparotomy (embolectomy/revascularization + resection of dead bowel, second look); NOMI → treat the cause, intra-arterial vasodilators (papaverine).
  • Chronic mesenteric ischaemia → postprandial pain and weight loss. 437

Systemic Anticoagulation

Slide 20
  • Goals of Anticoagulation
  • Decrease risk of thrombus propagation
  • Prevent recurrent embolization
  • Unfractionated heparin
  • Bolus dose 80 units /kg
  • Continuous infusion 18 units /kg/hr
  • Immediate after diagnosis
  • Blood investigation and sampling before start
  • Hold only if early angiography available
Notes

Investigation & Immediate Management

Classic acute embolic ALIAcute-on-chronic ischemia
First stepIV heparin (systemic anticoagulation)IV heparin
ImagingDo not delay revascularization for routine imaging; examination and pulses usually localize the level. CTA only if time and limb viability allow (e.g. OR unavailable) and it won't delay treatment.Usually needed: disease may involve extensive atherosclerosis and multiple stenotic segments. Investigate to plan the intervention.
RevascularizationUrgent clot removalAngioplasty or bypass rather than simple clot removal
Time availableNone: limb is threatened nowCollaterals + viable limb may allow time; urgency depends on ischemia severity

EXAM RULE

Classic acute embolic limb ischemia → immediate IV heparin + urgent revascularization. Imaging must never delay treatment of a clearly threatened limb.

Notes

Revascularization

Fogarty Balloon Embolectomy (open)

1 Expose the common femoral artery (± SFA & profunda)→2 Perform an arteriotomy→3 Pass the Fogarty catheter beyond the clot, balloon deflated→4 Inflate the balloon→5 Withdraw → extract embolus / thrombus→6 Restore flow, close the arteriotomy

Common femoral exposure can retrieve thrombus from proximal iliac or distal segments, depending on where it lies.

Open Embolectomy vs Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis

Open embolectomy / thrombectomyCatheter-directed thrombolysis (endovascular)
HowArteriotomy; Fogarty balloon pulls the clot outCatheter advanced into the thrombus; local tPA
DurationSingle operationInfusion for ~12 h, then reassessment / repeat angiography
Typical useCommon treatment for acute embolic occlusionSelected patients: unfit for open surgery, acute-on- chronic disease
Why this routeImmediate clot extractionLocal delivery avoids the large systemic dose a big thrombus would need → less bleeding risk

CHOOSING

Endovascular vs open depends on the patient's condition, the arterial pathology and the severity of ischemia.

Compartment Syndrome

DEFINITION

Raised pressure inside a closed fascial compartment → impaired tissue microcirculation → muscle ischemia / necrosis.

The leg has 4 fascial compartments

Each holds muscles with their vessels and nerves, wrapped in strong, relatively non-stretchable fascia.
Anterior·Lateral
Swelling inside a compartment raises pressure because the fascia cannot expand enough.
Superficial posterior·Deep posterior
Pressure is measured with an intracompartmental pressure needle.

Compartment pressure

10–12 mmHg Normal·15–18 mmHg Possible with muscular build / activity
>25 mmHg
Concerning (25–30+); lecturer's threshold is >25

Causes

Ischemia-reperfusion after revascularization
Fractures
Prolonged immobilization
Venous outflow obstruction
External compression, e.g. unconscious / comatose patient

The vicious cycle after reperfusion

Clinical findings

Severe pain
Tense swelling; firm, tight compartment
Pulses may remain present (see below)
Prolonged ischemia → muscle injury→Reperfusion swelling→Non-compliant fascia can't expand →·↑ Compartment pressure→↓ Muscle perfusion → more ischemia & necrosis

EXAM TRAP: PULSES DO NOT EXCLUDE COMPARTMENT SYNDROME

Compartment syndrome compromises the muscle microcirculation, not necessarily the main artery. Arterial pressure exceeds compartment pressure, so the artery keeps flowing:

Arterial pressure ~100–130 mmHg

pulse / Doppler signal preserved

Compartment pressure ~25–40 mmHg

microcirculation fails

A palpable pulse or positive arterial Doppler does NOT exclude compartment syndrome.

Vascular Emergencies · Study Guide

TREATMENT: EMERGENCY FASCIOTOMY

Surgically open the fascia to decompress the compartments. Sometimes done prophylactically after revascularization, particularly with:

Prolonged ischemia

Significant reperfusion swelling

Large / muscular lower limbs

Decision rests on ischemia duration, limb examination and clinical judgment.

Ischemia-Reperfusion Syndrome

Without flow, ischemic tissue accumulates metabolites. Restoring flow washes them suddenly into the venous circulation.

Accumulated substanceEffect on reperfusionPrepare / treat
PotassiumHyperkalemia: can be rapid and fatalInsulin + glucose, salbutamol (Ventolin), further urgent hyperkalemia management
Lactic acidMetabolic acidosisSodium bicarbonate for significant acidosis
Other toxic breakdown productsCardiac complications, incl. potentially fatal arrhythmiasAnticipate before flow is restored

BEFORE RELEASING THE CLAMPS

Coordinate with anesthesia before restoring blood flow: severe hyperkalemia and acidosis can develop immediately.

Rhabdomyolysis

Part of ischemia-reperfusion injury, considered separately because of its renal complications.

Ischemic skeletal Myoglobin released muscle breakdown → on reperfusion MONITOR AFTER REVASCULARIZATION • Serum creatinine • Urine output • Urine color: very dark from myoglobinuria→Myoglobin reaches Acute tubular injury → → Acute kidney injury the kidneys / necrosis TREAT • IV hydration to reduce kidney injury • Monitor and correct hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis
Notes

Mastery Checklist: Acute Limb Ischemia

1

Embolism vs acute-on-chronic: an embolus hits a normal artery with no collaterals → sudden, severe ischemia. Acute-on-chronic has collaterals → milder, atypical, may lack the full 6 Ps.

2

6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness and coldness come early; paresthesia precedes paralysis. Paralysis = advanced, possibly irreversible ischemia → amputation risk.

3

Pulse localization: femoral present / distal absent → femoropopliteal; one femoral absent → ipsilateral iliac; both absent → aortic bifurcation.

4

Classic embolic ALI → IV heparin + urgent revascularization, no delay for imaging. Acute-on-chronic → heparin, image, then angioplasty or bypass.

5

Fogarty embolectomy (open, via common femoral) vs catheter-directed thrombolysis (local tPA ~12 h; less bleeding than systemic lysis).

6

Compartment syndrome after reperfusion: pressure >25 mmHg, tense painful compartment, and pulses do not exclude it → fasciotomy.

7

Reperfusion washout: K⁺ (hyperkalemia, arrhythmia) and lactic acid (acidosis) → warn anesthesia before clamp release; myoglobin → AKI → IV fluids, watch for dark urine.

Arterial Aneurysms & AAA

Define it by diameter, tell true from false, then manage AAA by one goal: repair before rupture, once rupture risk outweighs procedural risk.

Slide 45
  • False Aneurysm
  • Disruption of arterial wall with presence of blood flow out side of normal layers of arterial wall.
  • Wall of false aneurysm is composed of compressed surrounding tissue
Notes

Definition & Classification

RULE OF THUMB

1.0 cm

Aneurysm = localized or diffuse arterial dilatation >50% above the normal expected diameter (≥1.5 × normal). Normal 1 cm → 1.3 cm is ectasia / dilatation, not an

aneurysm; 1.5 cm or more is an aneurysm. Matters on CT: not every enlarged artery is an aneurysm.

Normal

True vs False (Pseudo) Aneurysm

True aneurysmFalse aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)
What it isDilatation of the native arterial wallContained hematoma with persistent communication / flow from the artery
Wall of the sacThe arterial wall itselfFibrous tissue, not normal arterial wall
ShapesFusiform: circumferential Saccular: outpouching of part of the circumferenceSac connected to the artery through a defect
Classic exampleDegenerative AAAPuncture site after cardiac catheterization fails to seal → continued flow into a contained hematoma
Key distinctionIf bleeding stops and no communication persists → it is a hematoma, not a pseudoaneurysm
  • Local complication of angiography/angioplasty → pseudoaneurysm (at the puncture site). 438

Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)

Anatomy & Common Site

Aorta: ascending → arch → descending thoracic → abdominal (diaphragm to aortic bifurcation).
AAAs are described by their relation to the renal / visceral arteries: suprarenal / visceral, juxtarenal, infrarenal.
Infrarenal = the most common aneurysm location.
Exact location matters: operative approach, treatment indications and technical considerations all differ.

Vascular Emergencies · Study Guide

ETIOLOGY

Degenerative: most common (lecture focus)
Infection
Inflammatory disease
Connective tissue disorders
Trauma

The exact cause of degenerative aneurysm formation is not fully established; several risk factors are recognized.

AAA Risk Factors

Smoking
Hypertension
Hyperlipidemia
Atherosclerosis
Increasing age
Male sex
Race / ethnicity: higher in White populations, lower in populations of African ancestry
Family history, especially a first-degree relative

EXAM TRAP: DIABETES

Diabetes is NOT a typical AAA risk factor: epidemiological studies show an inverse / protective association.

FAMILY HISTORY DRIVES SCREENING

Strong enough to shape screening in some countries: an affected parent may prompt ultrasound screening of first-degree relatives, even with no identified connective tissue disorder.

Notes

90–95%

asymptomatic, found

incidentally

Picked up on ultrasound or CT done for something else, e.g. renal stones, biliary disease, gynecological complaints.
Occasionally felt as a pulsatile abdominal mass.
Patients may have no complaints at vascular referral; management aims to prevent rupture.

Symptomatic AAA: abdominal pain, back pain, or both (the abdominal aorta lies anterior to the vertebral column). Rarely, a large aneurysm compresses neighbors:

Compressed structureResult
IVC / iliac veinsVenous obstruction → DVT

RULE

These symptoms in a patient with AAA and no alternative explanation make the aneurysm symptomatic, even without rupture.

  • Elderly woman with AF, severe abdominal pain, WBC 24, lactate 8 → bowel (mesenteric) ischaemia. 442 ×24

AAA Management

Surveillance vs Repair

THE TRADE-OFF

Management depends on size, progression, symptoms and rupture risk.
Small, asymptomatic AAA → surveillance with ultrasound or CT.
Repair (open or endovascular) carries procedural risk, so its benefit must outweigh the risk of rupture; rupture risk rises with diameter.

Vascular Emergencies · Study Guide

Four Indications for Repair

≥5.5 cm in men → elective repair. Women: lower threshold, about ≥5.0 cm. 5.5 cm is the main exam threshold.·1 · Size·ELECTIVE·Expansion of >5 mm within 6 months is concerning and may indicate repair. Why growth rate is tracked at surveillance.·2 · Rapid growth·CONSIDER REPAIR·Unexplained abdominal / back pain or compression attributable to the AAA. Admit; urgent repair, potentially within 2–3 days. No size threshold needed.·3 · Symptomatic·URGENT·Immediate emergency management and operative repair.·4 · Rupture·EMERGENCY

Risk of Rupture

Small (<5.5 cm)
Low rupture risk → surveillance
≥5.5 cm Rupture risk now outweighs repair risk·7 cm Very high: ~70% (lecture figure)

PRINCIPLE

Delaying repair of a small asymptomatic aneurysm avoids procedural risk while rupture risk is low; repair becomes beneficial as rupture risk rises. Lecture figures are estimates, not individualized probabilities.

Repair Options

Open surgical repairEndovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR)
AccessLaparotomyFemoral arteries
TechniqueExpose the aneurysm; insert a vascular graft with proximal and distal anastomosesAdvance and deploy a stent graft inside the aorta to exclude the aneurysm
LimitationTraditional open operation with procedural riskNeeds suitable anatomy: not every aneurysm is appropriate for EVAR

Rupture AAA

Slide 58
  • Emergency
  • Clinical diagnosis – classic diagnostic triad- 50%
  • sudden onset back pain
  • shock
  • pulsatile mass
  • US in emergency or CT if stable
  • ABC – Cross match
  • Emergency repair
  • 100% mortality if untreated
  • OR mortality rate 50%
  • Pulsatile mass behind the knee (popliteal aneurysm) — the most significant complication → thrombosis and distal embolization (rupture is rare). 442 ×2
Notes

Ruptured AAA

EMERGENCY

Presentation

Sudden, severe abdominal and / or back pain
Hemorrhagic / hypovolemic shock: hypotension, tachycardia, possible loss of consciousness

Management

Immediate ABC assessment and resuscitation
Urgent transfer for open or endovascular repair without unnecessary delay

REMEMBER

The purpose of elective AAA repair is to prevent rupture, not to treat an otherwise asymptomatic dilatation.

Added explanationSMA territory: jejunum, ileum, caecum, ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. Chronic mesenteric ischaemia ("intestinal angina"): postprandial abdominal pain + food fear + weight loss. Ischaemic colitis: elderly, LLQ pain and bloody diarrhoea, watershed areas (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid).
Notes

Mastery Checklist: Aneurysms & AAA

1

Aneurysm = ≥1.5 × normal diameter (>50% above expected). 1.0 → 1.3 cm is ectasia, not an aneurysm.

2

True aneurysm involves the arterial wall (fusiform or saccular); a pseudoaneurysm is a contained hematoma with ongoing arterial communication and a fibrous wall (e.g. catheter puncture site).

3

Most common site: infrarenal aorta. Most common cause: degenerative.

Vascular Emergencies · Study Guide

4

Risk factors: smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atherosclerosis, age, male sex, White ethnicity, family history. Diabetes is protective.

5

90–95% asymptomatic. Symptomatic = abdominal / back pain or compression (DVT, bowel obstruction, hydronephrosis) without another cause.

6

Four repair indications: ≥5.5 cm (men; ~5.0 cm women), >5 mm growth in 6 months, symptomatic (urgent, 2– 3 days), rupture (emergency).

7

Ruptured AAA = pain + shock → ABC and straight to repair. EVAR needs suitable anatomy; open repair is via laparotomy with a graft.

Carotid Artery Disease

Carotid atherosclerosis causes neurological events mainly by throwing emboli, not by limiting flow. Treatment targets symptomatic, still-patent stenosis to prevent the next event.

Notes

Definition & Pathophysiology

DEFINITION

Carotid artery disease = atherosclerosis of the carotid arteries: the same systemic process as peripheral arterial disease (peripheral arteries) and coronary artery disease (coronary arteries). Shared risk factors include diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidemia, grouped as modifiable vs non-modifiable.

Why Carotid Disease Differs from PAD

Carotid diseasePeripheral arterial disease
Arterial supplyBrain fed by 2 carotids + 2 vertebrals; collaterals compensate, so even significant stenosis may cause no symptoms from low flow aloneCollaterals develop around chronic stenoses
PlaqueSuperficial portion often soft / vulnerableOften heavily calcified / hard
Typical plaque siteCarotid bifurcation / proximal ICAPeripheral arteries
Main mechanism of symptomsArtery-to-artery microembolizationReduced flow (ischemia)

ICA VS ECA ON IMAGING

The internal carotid artery has no branches in the neck; the external carotid gives branches in the neck. A useful way to tell them apart on vascular imaging.

Mechanism of Neurological Events

Carotid stenosis→↑ Flow velocity through the narrowed lumen→Soft plaque fragments detach→Microemboli “showerˮ downstream→Brain: stroke / TIA Retina: amaurosis fugax

EXAM-IMPORTANT

Carotid disease causes neurological events mainly through artery-to-artery microembolization, not simply reduced blood flow from the stenosis.

Complete Occlusion vs Severe Stenosis

Severe stenosis (e.g. 90–99%)Complete ICA occlusion
Flow over the plaqueStill present across an unstable plaqueNone: no residual lumen
Embolic riskContinuesPlaque material has nowhere to pass
Carotid endarterectomyMay be warranted if symptomaticGenerally not performed

GOAL OF INTERVENTION

Carotid intervention aims to prevent future neurological events; it does not reverse an established stroke.

Classification & Clinical Presentation

Carotid disease is classified as symptomatic or asymptomatic. The three symptomatic presentations:

Focal neurological deficit lasting ≥24 hours†. The lecture uses the traditional time-based definitions.·Transient focal deficit that resolves within 24 hours†.
Sudden, temporary monocular visual loss from retinal ischemia, in the ipsilateral eye. Vision returns in minutes to hours (lecture examples: ~30 min–2 h).
Stroke·TIA
Amaurosis fugax

MEMORY HOOK

Eye = same side, body = opposite side. The retina is supplied from the same-side ICA (via its ophthalmic branch), while the motor and sensory pathways from that hemisphere cross to the opposite side of the body.

  • Transient right-hand weakness for 1 hour + 80% left ICA stenosis → presentation = transient ischaemic attack. 439 ×6

Treatment

ScenarioManagement
Symptomatic (stroke, TIA, amaurosis fugax) + >50% ipsilateral stenosisConsider carotid intervention, particularly carotid endarterectomy (CEA)
Symptomatic + <50% stenosis†Best medical therapy (antiplatelet, statin, risk-factor control)†
Asymptomatic stenosis†Best medical therapy; CEA only for selected high-grade stenosis (guidelines commonly use 60–70%)†
Complete ICA occlusionNo endarterectomy: nothing left to embolize through

Stroke
Cranial nerve injury: e.g. hypoglossal nerve → tongue deviates to the ipsilateral (operated) side
Neck hematoma that can threaten the airway

Mastery Checklist: Carotid Artery Disease

1

Carotid events come mainly from microembolization of soft plaque, not reduced flow: the brain has collateral supply from 2 carotids + 2 vertebrals.

2

Plaque forms at the bifurcation / proximal ICA. The ICA has no neck branches; the ECA does.

3

Symptomatic = stroke, TIA, amaurosis fugax. TIA resolves within 24 h; amaurosis fugax is transient monocular visual loss.

4

Laterality: limb deficits are contralateral; amaurosis fugax is ipsilateral.

5

Duplex ultrasound (not Doppler alone) is the preferred test; it grades stenosis by velocity.

6

Symptomatic >50% → CEA. Complete occlusion → no CEA. Intervention prevents future events; it doesn't reverse a stroke.

7

CEA complications: stroke, hypoglossal injury (tongue deviates toward the operated side), airway- threatening neck hematoma.
